title: Washington Is Quietly Dismantling Every Path Indians Used to Stay in America
excerpt: Green card rules rewritten, student visas capped, Day 1 CPT under siege. 30,000 Indian students have already left. Germany and the UK are picking up the pieces.
body:
First, the Trump administration said immigrants on temporary visas must go home to apply for green cards. Then it proposed ending the system that lets international students stay for the duration of their studies. Now it wants to crack down on the programmes that let H-1B lottery losers keep working legally while they wait for another shot.

Taken together, these policies amount to the most systematic dismantling of Indian immigration pathways in a generation — and the numbers are already telling the story. **30,000 Indian students left the United States in the past year** without completing their courses, dropping the total from 382,000 to 352,000. US education consultants warn that as many as 70,000 more could leave in the coming year.

## The Adjustment of Status Blow

On May 22, the US Citizenship and Immigration Services issued a policy memo that immigration lawyers are calling a seismic shift. Until now, a foreign national already living legally in the US — say, on an H-1B work visa — could apply for a green card without leaving the country, through a process called **adjustment of status**. It was routine, predictable, and the basis on which hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals planned their lives.

USCIS has now declared that adjustment of status is "an extraordinary form of relief and administrative grace" — not the default pathway. The agency is directing its officers to push applicants toward **consular processing**, which means returning to their home country to complete the green card application at a US embassy.

"From now on, an alien who is in the US temporarily and wants a Green Card must return to their home country to apply, except in extraordinary circumstances," USCIS spokesman Zach Kahler said in the agency's announcement.

For the estimated 400,000-plus Indians stuck in the employment-based green card backlog — some with wait times stretching past 100 years — this is not a minor procedural change. It introduces a new layer of uncertainty into a system that was already punishing in its delays. Flying back to India for consular processing means leaving a job, pulling children out of school, and risking re-entry complications — all while the underlying backlog remains untouched.



> **"USCIS has now declared that adjustment of status is "an extraordinary form of relief and administrative grace" — not the default pathway."**


## The Student Visa Squeeze

The adjustment of status memo arrived on top of an already hostile environment for Indian students. The Department of Homeland Security has proposed replacing the longstanding "Duration of Status" system for F-1 visas — which allowed students to stay as long as they were enrolled — with a **fixed cap of four years**. Extensions would require approval from USCIS, adding bureaucratic uncertainty to every semester.

The same proposal would cut the grace period after F-1 status ends from 60 to 30 days, compress the window for securing a job or an H-1B sponsorship, and crack down on **Day 1 CPT programmes** — the pathway that allowed graduates who lost the H-1B lottery to enrol in another degree programme while continuing to work.

"For anyone who already has a master's degree, they are not going to be able to go back and say, 'I need another master's degree because I need work authorisation to continue working,'" immigration attorney Danielle Goldman told The Indian Eye. "There's no doubt that this is going to have a massive impact on the companies that are in desperate need of top talent."

Indians represent roughly half of all participants in OPT and STEM OPT, the post-study work programmes that make a US degree worth the six-figure investment many families take out loans — and sometimes mortgages — to finance.

## The Green Card Backlog Tightens

Meanwhile, the June 2026 Visa Bulletin delivered another setback: EB-2 India retrogressed by more than 10 months, and EB-1 India — the category for people of "extraordinary ability" — retrogressed by three months. The State Department warned that further retrogressions, or even categories becoming "unavailable," may occur before the fiscal year ends in September.

The combined effect is a system where getting *in* is harder, staying *in* is more uncertain, and the pathway to permanence is longer and more perilous than at any point in recent memory.

## Where They're Going Instead

The exodus is already reshaping global talent flows. **Germany** has emerged as the biggest beneficiary, with Indian student numbers surging from 28,905 in 2023 to 59,400 in 2026 — making Indians the largest international student group in the country, ahead of Chinese students. Public universities in Germany, France, and the Netherlands offer free or heavily subsidised education, and several European countries allow graduates to stay for up to two years after completing their studies.

Canada, once the default alternative, has tightened too. Under Prime Minister Mark Carney, international student arrivals dropped 60%, and Indian students now account for just 8% of the total — down from 52% in 2023.

The UK, by contrast, has been actively courting Indian talent. The India-UK trade deal going live on July 15 includes provisions for professional mobility, and the Graduate Route visa continues to offer a two-year post-study work window.

## The Diaspora Dilemma

For the 4.4 million Indians in the United States, these policy shifts cut at the foundation of how the community was built. The Indian-American story is, overwhelmingly, an immigration story — families who came on student visas, transitioned to H-1Bs, waited years for green cards, and eventually became citizens. Each of the pathways that made that journey possible is now narrower than it was a year ago.

The question is whether this represents a temporary political overcorrection that a future administration will reverse, or the new normal. For the generation currently making the decision about where to build their lives, the answer cannot wait.

*Sources: USCIS policy memo PM-602-0199 (May 22, 2026), The Indian Eye, ICEF Monitor, Lexology, Bhaskar English, WR Immigration*
